rules.surface_condition: cuts where the token immediately after the marker is a clause-introducing auxiliary/causal/negation token that often starts a continuation (these tokens often indicate the remainder can overturn or continue the left):
rules.blamed_rule: - Is the token immediately after the marker a determiner/preposition/auxiliary/relative pronoun? If yes, bias score downward.
rules.proposed_rule: In [Scoring Rules]: if the token immediately after the marker is one of {because, causing, because, since, as, due, because, then, no, not, because, therefore, hence, so, therefore} or is a finite/copular/auxiliary token that launches a clause (one of {was, were, is, are, be, been, being, had, have, has}), reduce the score substantially — put the marker into a low target band (5–30). This should OVERRIDE any generic upward bias coming from a reliable-looking token on the left (names, numerals, quoted noun-phrases). Rationale: many measured failures arise when a lexical left fragment looks good but what follows is a causal/auxiliary continuation that overturns or completes it; lowering avoids over-trust.

rules.surface_condition: cuts where the token immediately after the marker is a predicate/finite verb that continues the main clause (i.e., the marker would separate a noun/subject chunk from its verb), e.g. won/want/reach/serve/show/succeed
rules.blamed_rule: - Cuts that separate two independently meaningful lexical clusters (e.g., noun phrase + independent verb phrase) where both clusters contain content words (nouns, verbs, numerals) and do not leave a dangling single function word are likely to score higher.
rules.proposed_rule: In [Scoring Rules]: when the token immediately after the marker is a finite/main-verb (examples below) and the token immediately before the marker is contentful (noun, name, numeral, or an NP-like left chunk), reduce the score moderately (target band 10–40). Rationale: the model currently over-values cuts that isolate a lexical left chunk from the verb that completes it (subjects/objects separated from predicates); measured labels show such splits often produce poor right-side translatability or contradiction.

rules.surface_condition: cuts where the token immediately before the marker is a demonstrative pronoun (this/that/these/those) and the token immediately after is a noun (a common pattern where the left chunk ('... this') is a reliable short chunk and the right is the head noun), i.e. markers of the form 'this | noun' or 'that | noun'
rules.blamed_rule: - Is the token immediately before the marker a numeral/date/percentage/name? If yes, bias score upward.
rules.proposed_rule: In [Scoring Rules]: raise the score (move toward a higher band, target band 55–85) when left_last is a demonstrative pronoun {this, that, these, those} AND right_first is a lexical noun (examples below). Rationale: the measurer often finds short demonstrative fragments translate reliably on their own and the right noun phrase also translates well; examples show the model sometimes under-ranks these boundaries.

summary: The model still over-values lexical-looking left fragments even when what follows is a clause that negates/continues them (causal auxiliaries, causing/ because/was/etc.). It also over-trusts cuts that separate subject/NP from the predicate (finite verbs). Conversely, the model under-ranks cuts after demonstratives (this/that) that empirical measurement shows are often good. The proposed rules (1) force a strong downward override when clause-introducing auxiliaries/causatives/negations follow, (2) lower cuts that separate an NP from a following finite verb, and (3) raise cuts after demonstratives followed by nouns.
